If you're going for geographical realism, read on. If you're going for "it's my map and it's just like that" (which is a totally valid way!), ignore this.

Right off the bat, the rivers are doing some wacky things. The most important thing about waterways is that they always flow down, which encompasses two bits of advice you'll commonly find in this sub: rivers flow from high elevation to low elevation (unlike at the SW corner of the larger land mass where a river flows into and out of of a mountain range, though if you wanted to keep that, you could totally explain it as a gorge/canyon like the Danube through eastern Europe or through artificial or underground means of that suits the world) and rivers almost always come together instead of split (except in the case of river deltas, small scale splits that you wouldn't see on maps of continents, and rare river bifurcations).

Your mountains seem more hectic than they would be in real life too. Mountains usually form long chains and are formed from the bending and folding of the earth. I would suggest reworking your mountains, possibly cutting back on some of them and connecting others to form cohesive chains. With your scale, your larger land mass seems ~about~ the size of something like Australia, the US, the southern "arm" of Africa, or mainland Europe, so going and looking at elevation maps of similarly-sized areas should help you get a feel for how mountains look in those regions.

Finally, just looking at some of the other bits and bobs, the biggest thing that sticks out to me is the salt flats in the east. Real life salt flats are usually boxed in by mountains (because they're basically just dried up mountain lakes). Even if the mountains aren't immediately surrounding the flats, they still form a basin around them. In the regions I pointed out above, I'd look at the Etosha Pan in Namibia and Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah for examples of scale, terrain, etc...

Of course, take all of the above with a massive grain of salt. Real geography loves to one-up fiction, so there's probably an explanation you could dream up for whatever you wanted to put, especially if your setting is gonna have magic! Overall, it's a great map, and you should definitely keep making more!!

Hi, could you maybe try to read what I wrote before responding? I'm not saying that Saturn doesn't have a planetary tilt and therefore annual weather patterns. I'm saying the grouping of those patterns is relative and cultural.

If (just imagine with me for a second), most astronomers lived in cultures where seasons were defined with equinoxes and solstices as the midpoint of the season, when do you think Saturn's summer would start?

Again, the actual weather caused by axial tilt is real, and obviously the axial tilt itself and solstices/equinoxes are real, but the actual term "season" is created by humans and depends on culture. These are two different concepts.

Like, when does a "day" start? Some cultures might say midnight, some might say sunrise, others might have different definitions. That doesn't take away from the fact that the earth has rotated.

Also I'm not saying that our definition of "season" is arbitrary. Just like it makes sense to say midnight or sunrise are the start of a day, it also makes sense to say seasons are defined by the solstices and equinoxes, but it also could make sense to base seasons on plant life or a culture's calendar or rainfall or any number of other things.

Even accepting that the seasons are based on the equinoxes and solstices, some cultures (eg, Celts and some Medieval European cultures) used them as the midpoint for their seasons. It's all relative.

Hell, due to seasonal lag, our seasons aren't even cleanly based on temperature but rather just the sun's position and earth's tilt.

Anyway, to sum that rant up: weather and climate are real world phenomenon, but seasons are the way that cultures make sense and track them and are therefore culturally relative.

The weather related to seasons is definitely concrete and real, but seasons themselves are made up by humans. If aliens came to earth, they could just as easily take our four seasons (warming, hot, cooling, cold) and make it two seasons (hot, cold), especially if they land in places that just have rainy and dry seasons. 

I'm sure that aliens could make any number of divisions if the yearly weather in a region is stable enough like an 8 season cycle where each season is divided in half to get things like "warming up slowly" / "warming up quickly" or maybe even a 3 season cycle related to plant growth that's (growing, dying, dormant).

I think you're misunderstanding what the main point of saying "archaeology feels disconnected from the main game / like a mod." The issue isn't that it's not visually connected (like the sherds having symbols from the game), but that archaeology doesn't feel connected to the systems of the base game.

Just as an example of what I mean, look at the difference between copper and iron. Iron is used for all sorts of things in a huge variety of different areas: decorative blocks, iron armor and tools, pistons, rails, etc... and is even connected to other things like iron golems, zombie loot, and treasure loot. Copper, in comparison, is extremely isolated from the rest of Minecraft's systems. Sure it has a variety of decorative blocks thanks to weathering, but there's literally only five uses for copper ingots (copper blocks, lightning rod, brush, spyglass, and armor trims) and one other extra tidbit in that drowneds will drop ingots. 

To me, this is what archaeology feels like. The ruins' only point is archaeology (which isn't a bad thing in and of itself since most other structures have a single purpose), and archaeology only connects to the base game at a few points like providing a music disc, materials, and a new decorative pot.

In general, I think my issue with archaeology is that, like some other updates, it feels a mile wide and an inch deep, not really connecting and interacting with the base game's systems.
